blocks.text: HarborWorks describes a site as a hierarchy: a root organization contains locations, locations contain racks, and racks contain machines. That ownership-shaped model is a tree only while each contained object has one parent and the relationships contain no cycles. A machine shared by two locations or a dependency pointing back to an ancestor requires a different model.

topics.title: 9.1.2 Measuring Height and Depth
topics.summary: Depth is the number of edges from the root to a node. This chapter measures height as the maximum number of edges from a node to a descendant leaf. A leaf therefore has height zero, and an empty tree is represented by height minus one for the recursive helper.

blocks.text: Some books count nodes rather than edges when defining height. Either convention can work if used consistently; mixing them causes off-by-one errors in base cases and balance formulas. State the convention next to the implementation rather than assuming every reader uses the same one. The empty sentinel also requires a result type that can represent minus one.

blocks.text: Depth measures distance from the root along edges. Height measures the longest downward distance to a leaf under this chapter’s convention. In the example, the root has depth zero and height two; its child containing two has depth one and height one; the grandchildren have depth two and height zero.

In the example, the root has depth zero and height two; its child containing two has depth one and height one; the grandchildren have depth two and height zero.

blocks.text: The empty-tree helper returns minus one so that a leaf’s height becomes 1 + max(empty-child heights) in an equivalent binary formulation. This is a convention that simplifies a recurrence, not a physical negative distance. Chapter 11 deliberately uses node-count height with empty zero and leaf one for AVL metadata. The two conventions are consistent within their own formulas but differ by one for nonempty trees.

blocks.text: State a convention before writing a validator. An assertion expecting leaf height one will falsely reject a correctly implemented edge-count height zero. Such an off-by-one is a specification mismatch, not necessarily a traversal bug. Printed diagrams should label whether numbers represent depth from root or height to leaves; they are not interchangeable on an unbalanced tree.

blocks.text: The height recurrence follows the dependency structure. A node cannot know its own height until the heights of its children have been computed. Each child contributes a candidate downward path; the longest is chosen, then the edge from the node to that child is counted. This is an example of bottom-up aggregation and prepares the reader for postorder processing.

blocks.text: Shape affects resources. A chain of n nodes has height n-1 and can create linear recursion depth. A broad shallow tree can have small height but a large breadth-first queue. The number of nodes alone does not determine which auxiliary resource becomes large. Draw a chain and a star to expose the two extremes.

topics.title: 9.2 Traversing Trees
topics.summary: Depth-first traversal follows a branch before moving to later siblings. Breadth-first traversal processes all nodes at one depth before the next. Their data structures differ: recursion or an explicit stack for depth-first work, a queue for breadth-first work.

blocks.text: The recursive implementations process each node once, giving linear traversal work in the number of nodes. Auxiliary call-stack depth is proportional to tree height, while the returned output vector itself contains one value per node. A very deep untrusted hierarchy can exceed call-stack limits; an explicit stack or bounded-depth ingestion policy is needed for that broader domain.

blocks.text: Depth-first traversal completes a branch before moving to the next sibling branch. Preorder records the current node before descending, while postorder records it after all children. The same child order can therefore produce different valid outputs depending on when the node is visited.

blocks.text: For a root one with children two and three, and children four and five beneath two, preorder is one, two, four, five, three. Postorder is four, five, two, three, one. Both contain the same five node visits. Their usefulness differs because their dependency ordering differs.

blocks.text: Preorder suits a parent-first outline or propagation of inherited context. Postorder suits computing a total from child totals, such as a subtree’s record count. A deletion or cleanup procedure often needs children handled before the parent’s owning state disappears, but the exact lifetime behavior of C++ members must still be considered rather than inferred from a traversal name.
rich: Preorder suits a parent-first outline or propagation of inherited context. Postorder suits computing a total from child totals, such as a subtree’s record count. A deletion or cleanup procedure often needs children handled before the parent’s owning state disappears, but the exact lifetime behavior of C++ members must still be considered rather than inferred from a traversal name.

blocks.text: A recursive call stores unfinished work: after returning from one child, the function must continue with the next child and eventually finish the parent. An explicit stack can model that work. For preorder, pushing children in reverse order preserves the original left-to-right visit order when they are later popped. For postorder, a frame can remember the node and next child index, or a second state can mark that children have been scheduled.

For postorder, a frame can remember the node and next child index, or a second state can mark that children have been scheduled.

blocks.text: Do not duplicate visits accidentally while converting recursion. Pushing every child and then recursively visiting those same children mixes two control strategies. Compare the complete output against a hand trace and check that each node identity appears exactly once. Equal stored values make identity-based validation more informative than value counts alone.

blocks.text: The returned vector is part of memory usage. Even with a shallow recursion stack, collecting every visit requires linear output storage. A callback-based traversal can avoid that particular result vector, but then callback failure, mutation, and lifetime rules become part of the interface. The simplest complete example makes one clear tradeoff at a time.

Depth-first traversal completes a branch before moving to the next sibling branch. Preorder records the current node before descending, while postorder records it after all children. The same child order can therefore produce different valid outputs depending on when the node is visited.

For a root one with children two and three, and children four and five beneath two, preorder is one, two, four, five, three. Postorder is four, five, two, three, one. Both contain the same five node visits. Their usefulness differs because their dependency ordering differs.

Preorder suits a parent-first outline or propagation of inherited context. Postorder suits computing a total from child totals, such as a subtree’s record count. A deletion or cleanup procedure often needs children handled before the parent’s owning state disappears, but the exact lifetime behavior of C++ members must still be considered rather than inferred from a traversal name.

A recursive call stores unfinished work: after returning from one child, the function must continue with the next child and eventually finish the parent. An explicit stack can model that work. For preorder, pushing children in reverse order preserves the original left-to-right visit order when they are later popped. For postorder, a frame can remember the node and next child index, or a second state can mark that children have been scheduled.

Do not duplicate visits accidentally while converting recursion. Pushing every child and then recursively visiting those same children mixes two control strategies. Compare the complete output against a hand trace and check that each node identity appears exactly once. Equal stored values make identity-based validation more informative than value counts alone.

The returned vector is part of memory usage. Even with a shallow recursion stack, collecting every visit requires linear output storage. A callback-based traversal can avoid that particular result vector, but then callback failure, mutation, and lifetime rules become part of the interface. The simplest complete example makes one clear tradeoff at a time.

blocks.text: Review reasoning. Why does BFS not need visited state here? The model is a tree with one ownership path per node. Why can its queue be large despite shallow height? A broad level contains many pending nodes. Why can a child reference survive vector growth? The separately allocated child does not move with its owner. Why is postorder useful for aggregation? Child results exist before the parent combines them. Why is an explicit stack not free? It still stores pending control state, just in a visible container.
